utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, good morning, Your Honour. This is case number IT-03-67-PT, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Today is the 5th of June 2007. I'd like to greet all the people present in the courtroom, the representatives from the Prosecution, Mr. Seselj, and I would also like to welcome all the people present in the courtroom. On the agenda for today's Status Conference, we have a number of items which I'm about to address. One has to do with future schedule. I have planned to have a Status Conference on the 4th of July at 9.00. As you know, we will then have our summer recess, which means that there will be no hearings in July and at the beginning of the month of August. I shall resume with this trial on the 13th of August. This means that we shall meet again in the last week of August. So much for our schedule. I would also like to very briefly address another item, which has to do with the directive on the number of pages and the number of words. As you know, because of translation problems, the directive has had to set the number of pages and the number of words. This does lead to a number of problems sometimes and it has happened that the motions of the accused have been dismissed because the word count had been exceeded. In order to avoid this occurring again, and I would like to thank Mr. Seselj and his associates who have -- who are now in the habit when they are filing a longer motion, to state from the outset that they seek leave to extend their motion, which will go beyond the word and sentence limit. A motion which is ten pages long will, of course, represent a considerable amount of work for the translation unit, and this is why we did try to curtail the number of pages. We all know that we have to make a special effort to summarise what we wish to say, and sometimes it is possible to sum this up in a small number of pages. In certain circumstances, of course, one does need to have those extra pages. The third item I wanted to address had to do with a protocol on the registration of documents, protocol that has been recently adopted by the Registry and both Prosecution and Mr. Seselj have been notified of this. Why did this particular protocol come to life? When a motion is being filed by Mr. Seselj, this motion is drafted in Cyrillic, and nobody in the Registry can understand what this motion contains. In certain cases, an urgent request may be filed by Mr. Seselj which substantiates an immediate response. To avoid any malfunctioning, the procedure will be adopted as follows: As soon as the motion reaches the Registry, this will be notified and a date will be recorded. It will be specified that the Registry has received a document from the Defence, with an acknowledgement of receipt. This motion is then sent off to the translation unit. This may take several days, since you know that it takes one day for a translator to translate four pages which means that if a motion is a 15-page motion, this will take four days. When this kind of motion is filed, the translation unit reviews the content of the motion very quickly, and then sends a short summary of the content of the motion to the Chamber and to the Prosecution. The motion is then translated and registered, and the deadline starts running from the date on which the Registry has recorded the translated motion. Likewise, when a motion is filed by the Prosecution in English, the deadline only starts running once the motion has been translated in the language of the accused. This is a working principle, which means that we are all equal in these matters. Therefore, Mr. Seselj, if you have an urgent motion to file, which according to you calls for a very quick response, you should indicate this on your motion and write the word "urgent" on your motion so that has to be put on a priority list. Because if nothing is mentioned, there might not be a swift response because one feels that that might just be a standard motion. So it is important that you mention this because your motion will then be a priority. I also wanted to reassure you, during the summer recess in July and August, if you have an urgent motion to file, the motion will be processed either by me, because I will be permanently in contact with the legal officer or with the duty judge, because this Tribunal is working 24 hours a day and there will be a duty judge there who can respond to an urgent motion if need be. If that is the case, don't hesitate to write "urgent" across the motion so that it can be processed as a priority and that yet you don't have to suffer any adverse consequences. Now, as far as this protocol on recording of the documents is concerned, this was registered yesterday, and you will have a translation of this protocol in your own language very shortly, because this is quite a short protocol and it should not take too much time to translate. So much for the registration protocol. The fourth item I wish to address today has to do with the payment of fees of your assistants. As I indicated to you last time, Mr. Seselj, it is important that you prepare your motion and file your motion. I have, as yet, not received anything, and before giving you the floor on this matter, I would like to share with you the content of the letter which has been sent by the legal adviser of the United Nations, a letter that has been sent to the Registry on the 22nd of May. Let me read out paragraph 5 to you, which is, as far as we are concerned, the key paragraph. I shall read it out slowly so that you can hear it in your own language. "The bureau of legal affairs would nonetheless like to insist on the fact that an accused who would like his assistants, whether these be legal assistants or investigators, be remunerated by the Tribunal should prove that he does not have the means to pay them. Therefore, it is appropriate to apply the method commonly used to assess the financial means of the accused. This is done by the Registry. In addition, as the Appeals Chamber has indicated, the advisers should only be designated if the Registry is convinced that they meet those conditions set by it. This also applies to Defence counsel who are entitled to work for the Tribunal. They should also be entitled to control the expenses of the Defence, who is representing himself, before reimbursing him. The provisions of the direction on the assignment of Defence counsel, Directive number 1/14, and the Registry's policy with regard to financial matters would apply mutatis mutandis to the counsels of the accused who is representing himself." New York has therefore taken a stance on this which is in your favour, insofar as, in New York, they are saying that your counsel should be remunerated by the Tribunal, but of course under the condition that you are unable to pay them, in other words that you do not have such means that would enable you to pay them, and in addition, your counsel should meet the requirements and criteria adopted here, i.e., competence, ethical code, the standard requirements for any lawyer. And in addition, the registrar must then reimburse those expenses that have been incurred. Things are not very clear when we get to this particular point because we seem to be saying that if you don't have any money you should pay your counsels and then you will be reimbursed afterwards. So I think that this particular item is not really clear and requires further investigation because I don't see how it is possible, if you can't pay your counsels, how could you pay in advance unless you take out a loan with a bank and get reimbursed afterwards. So this requires further explanation. At the end of last week, I was informed of the content of this document, but I have not been able to organise a meeting with the Registry yet to see how we deal with this document in practical terms. This would amount to instructions given by the Secretary-General to the Registry of this Tribunal but notwithstanding that, I don't think this poses any particular obstacle because you can still file a motion and according to the Statute, be granted a number of facilities. I had strongly recommended you pursue this at our last Status Conference, and as I told you a while ago, I have not, as yet, received a motion from you or from any of your associates. I shall now give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Judge, our legal advisers have sent me the text of this motion to the Trial Chamber for a ruling binding the Registry to co-finance my defence. This was on Monday last week, which is eight days ago. This was sent by special mail, by DHL, as it's called. It was supposed to arrive in The Hague by Wednesday, latest. However, it was only submitted to me yesterday after I had pressed the matter with the detention authorities. As soon as I had read it, I signed the motion and I sent it back. It was sent to the Court from prison yesterday. I didn't do it as quickly as I would have liked to, or as perhaps you would have liked me to. However, there is an objective problem at stake there that I'm unable to solve for the time being, at least until my legal advisers move to The Hague and it's possible to send special air shipments to them and then they can forward these shipments to me in the Detention Unit the same day, and that is the only way I can think of to solve this matter. So the motion was submitted to me yesterday. Secondly, it is quite obvious that the -- that legal service of the United Nations has now reached the same position that I have been advocating for at least the last four years and which you too have confirmed as the right position, the correct position. The International Tribunal must be involved in co-financing my defence, at least to the extent that I'm unable to cover the costs. This is a final conclusion. Secondly, as far as my legal advisers are concerned, they have been rubber-stamped so to speak, registered by the Registry. They are qualified experts, although formally none of them, save for one, are lawyers. They have proven their qualifications by their work so far. You can't -- you won't be able to find a single counsel acting before this Tribunal who understands better the legal problems involved here and who writes better motions than my legal advisers. This fact is beyond dispute. I don't think there is any basis for anyone any more now to challenge the qualifications of my legal advisers. They are lawyers, graduate lawyers, some of them were practising lawyers, some were not, but they are certainly far more able than most of the lawyers and counsel acting before this Tribunal in other cases. The most important thing being I'm very satisfied with their work and with their qualifications. As far as the way in which this money will be paid is concerned, I wasn't quite clear about this myself after you had read the contribution from the legal adviser of the United Nations but I have no way of first paying my legal advisers and then later being refunded by the International Tribunal. I have no money to do that with. I declared all of my assets and all of my property back in 2003 when I filled all the forms given to me by the Tribunal, by the Registry. The Registry never challenged any of the information stated therein. They later wanted to know about my mother's property and my entire family lives in the house owned by my mother. I don't have a house of my own. My mother lives with her sisters and my sister in a house owned by my wife. I have four sons, two grandsons, one daughter-in-law. It's a huge family, so those two families are now living in one house. So that is the only property involved. My wife and my mother refuse to cooperate with the investigators of the ICTY. There is a man named Jovanovic, a Slovene person, who turned up, he's from Valjevo. My mother told him from the balcony that he's a disgusting person and she wasn't willing to cooperate. I could perhaps try to force my wife to cooperate but she is not bound in any way to follow any of my instructions. My mother does not wish to be involved. She says she was not involved in any crimes that I may have committed. She says she doesn't mind me committing possible crimes but she minds me not being better able to conceal them so no one is able to prosecute me. This may strike you a bit strange however cynicism is the only weapon I still have at my disposal, by way of a reaction to the actions of the Registry. The legal advisers of the UN only speak about me, about my rights and about my obligations but they don't dwell on my family and their responsibilities and obligations. There is no such right and no one else can be held accountable of my legal obligations, the legal obligations incumbent upon me, not even my children. No one else can be made responsible or held to account. Secondly, I have absolutely no option of taking out a loan with any bank. In order to do that I should be gainfully employed on a permanent basis, which I haven't been for the last five years so I have not been receiving a regular salary. As for my pension fund, money is being paid into it all the time because of the books being published all the time written by me, by the Serbian Radical Party. That is as much as they have been able to do for me. They have been paying money into my pension fund on a monthly basis because of these books being sold, and that's all. But based on that alone, I am still unable to take out a loan. I have no assets that I could use towards taking out this loan, and it is impossible for me to get any money from any bank. My legal advisers, therefore, have so far continued to work in the expectation that one day they would eventually be paid and so many years have gone by already. Assuming I had paid them already, the Registry should have given the money back to me. However, if I'd had the money to begin with, the Registry would never have had to be involved financially in my defence. As soon as I laid my hands on some money, the International Criminal Tribunal would no longer be under this obligation. Nothing would please me better than that. I wish there was some sort of a windfall, me ending up with a lot of money and not having to ask for this money from the International Tribunal. However that is just not an option. It is simply not possible. The only possibility is for the Registry to calculate the costs of my defence, stage by stage, starting with the pre-trial stage as it has evolved so far; the next pre-trial stage before the trial finally begins; the Prosecution case; the Defence case; and finally the appeals stage. This would be the only normal thing to do, the only normal course of action to take. In order for them to be able to do that, the Registry would first have to disclose information such as the following: What the costs have been of all the other Defences in all the other cases. That can be the only objective criterion that can be applied to my case. Let's see how complicated those cases were in relation to mine or as compared to mine. Save for the late Slobodan Milosevic, I'm the only accused being held to account for crimes possibly committed in three different countries. No one else is left facing a situation like that, which would seem to me that this is the most complicated case and thus the most expensive one in terms of setting up a defence. However the Registry seemed to be keeping secret information concerning the finances of defence teams in other cases, and if that is the case, there is nothing for us to discuss. If the Registry said, for example, we have rules and this is our calculation, but I refuse to talk to them like that until they disclose to me how they reached these figures. For example, if you have American lawyers acting in a case, their fees are different from those of Serbian lawyers, and they are paid earlier. That seems to be the established practice before this Tribunal. And this is just one of the many things that we have been made to face here in this so-called legal practice, and the procedures used by the Registry as a body of judicial administration which is under the authority of the judicial authorities which is the Trial Chamber. The Registry is not a judicial power, so to speak, they are a body of judicial administration, they are an executive body, they don't make the policies, only the Chambers do. The first instance Chambers, the Appellate Chamber, and the bureau of judges. The Registry must first say how much all the other defences have cost, how much the engagement of defence counsel Lazarevic has cost them, who was appointed to my case, how much van der Spoel has cost them, who picked for himself a team of assistants, and then also Hooper with his entire team, the counsel that was imposed on me. And then we can establish a set of criteria to see how the Defence has so far has been paid for. My legal advisers cannot be paid less money than van der Spoel or Hooper. This is simply impossible; I cannot allow for that. Hooper and O'Shea, who was his co-counsel, what they got per month, the sum total of what they got per month, should be given to my three associates and then split up between them. We must have these objective indicators. If we don't, nothing can be resolved. Therefore, the only way to go forward is for the Registry to use objective criteria, establish a certain sum, a sum that is deemed objective by any reasonable lawyer or legal expert, something that is reasonably acceptable, and then for this sum to be split up based on the involvement of certain members of the legal team or rather based on their expenses. What I would do in this case would be this alone. I would tell the Registry, this and that person, this and that sum is to be paid to this and that person into this or that account. Therefore, I would not be receiving any money at all in any of these situations. The money would be received directly by whoever was in charge of accomplishing a certain task. Once my legal advisers are involved in a permanent basis they would be paid a monthly salary here in The Hague and they would resign as far as their positions in Belgrade are concerned. They would leave their jobs and come here to work for me on a permanent basis and so would the case manager. That is the only way to go forward with this, and I don't know if there is any other way to work our way around this problem. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You have told me, sir, that the motion was drawn up on Wednesday. As soon as I will have been notified it, I will rule on it. I will also organise a working session swiftly with the Registry so as to draw the adequate consequences on the position given to us by the United Nations legal adviser in New York, saying that you are entitled to have remunerated legal advisers. I do believe that we will reach a solution very swiftly, and that indeed we will make it feasible for you to rule -- to organise your defence. Now I would now like to move on in closed session because we will be mentioning something directly related to what we have already mentioned. I will then give the floor to Accusation afterwards. The issue I want to mention now is in direct line of what we've just mentioned so, registrar, please closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in closed session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, we are now in closed session because you mentioned earlier your legal advisers, saying that they do a sterling job and I have indeed noticed it while reading their motions myself. It so happens, sir, that last week, and I'm sure you will have told -- you will have been told that, maybe slightly later on but I'm sure you will have been informed of it, one of your legal advisers, Mr. Aleksandar Vucic and a number of other people of your -- of his political party, went and took to the streets and put up a number of posters about Mr. Mladic. Now, as you know, Mr. Mladic is under formal investigation and he is indeed mentioned in your indictment as being involved in the criminal actions. So it so happens that one of your advisers, who should, all being well, be here in the courtroom with you at some point or other, and he has taken to the streets and been seen by the media to support an accused, someone who is under an indictment, and has been searched and -- by the Court for a number of years. Mr. Vucic had also said, in writing, that he would agree and -- agree to the rules of the Courts that he would be -- behave in an ethical manner. Now, my question, sir, is did you know about this? Would this possibly change your attitude vis-a-vis Mr. Vucic, and do you feel from your point of view, and I'm sure that accusation will also have something to say about this, do you not think that it has -- Prosecution, I mean, has something to say about this. Do you not think that it does not call into question the position of your legal adviser because, in fact, he is supporting Mr. Mladic, who is under investigation and for whom an arrest warrant has been circulated? So, sir, did you know about this or have you only just learned about it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Judge, I was informed in a timely manner of this event. Mr. Vucic signed the requisite document for the benefit of the Secretariat as he was being registered as a legal adviser. He has fully complied with all his obligations. However, his obligation is solely in relation to my case on the protection of confidential information in relation to this International Tribunal in a quite general sense. He never signed anything to the effect that he would cease all of his political activity. He's the secretary-general of the Serbian Radical Party, and the policy of the Serbian Radical Party from the very outset was to refuse to recognise the legality of this International Tribunal; to oppose the surrender of any of the accused Serbs to this Tribunal; and further, the policy of the Serbian Radical Party is that this International Tribunal is an instrument in the hands of Serb enemies, the United States of America, all the member states of the -- of NATO, and the EU. Mr. Vucic on the streets of Belgrade, lawfully and in keeping with the Serbian laws, made known, made public, his political positions. The Belgrade authorities wanted to change the name of this one particular boulevard and wanted the boulevard to now be named after the -- after the one major Mafia man in the Serbian history so far who was killed four years ago, Zoran Djindjic, the former president. We were against that as a political party. What happened is that some young people who were not members of our party put up posters of Ratko Mladic all along the boulevard. They were arrested and put in jail for seven months because of disrupting public order. This is against the law so our political party reacted in the following way: We went straight to the boulevard and we did the same thing all over again, this alleged violation, out of spite against the regime telling them come on, go ahead and arrest us, if you can. They couldn't because there was no crime to speak of to begin with. There was no violation of any of the laws and rules availing in Serbia. This was a manifestation of a political opinion, a choice. Mr. Vucic, when he's in this courtroom, will keep his position regarding the illegal nature of this International Tribunal. That is his private opinion, but he will not appear in this courtroom until I appear in my own case. So he and the other two legal advisers will be examining me during my Defence case and this will be the only moment throughout the entire trial that my legal advisers will address the Court, that is, when they are examining me in my future capacity as a witness, in my own case. So we are talking about his political convictions. I respect that. I happen to share these political convictions. My political conviction is that Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic must never face this Tribunal alive. This is their historical responsibility to the Serbian people because through them, the entire Serbian nation, the entire Serbian people, would be tried. My situation is different; I'm here to beat The Hague Tribunal, which I will do. They would never be able to. Other mechanisms would be used against them. They would be tried and convicted, and through them the Serbian people would be convicted because this is the policy pursued by the Western powers and the long-standing enemies of the Serbs. The members of the Radical Party will continue to work in Belgrade against The Hague Tribunal and that is something that concerns them and nobody else. Once Mr. Vucic is receiving a salary as a legal adviser in my case, he will resign to all his positions, from all his positions in Belgrade and spending most of his time here in The Hague. The only time he will appear to speak publicly will be as a member of my Defence team while upholding all the obligations that he assumed, to never disclose any of the protected witnesses or any sort of confidential information or protected documents by making those public. But you can't brainwash people. That is precisely why I trust my legal advisers, because they oppose The Hague Tribunal. You can't possibly be thinking that I would be able to trust legal advisers favouring The Hague Tribunal. I could never bring myself to trust such people. I'd rather die than allow such people to help me with my Defence. I think this is crystal clear. Never for a moment did the Serb Radical Party give up its anti-Hague policies. We didn't want to join Kostunica's government because he, in a manner of speaking, delivered himself to The Hague. He would like to have a coalition with us because we are the most powerful, the most consistent political party. He would rather have us than Tadic's people. This is what politics in Serbia are about right now. We have chosen the hardest way, by opposing the United States, NATO and the European Union, and we are prepared to pursue this path even if it costs us our lives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, on the political aspect that you have developed, you will understand that I will not comment. However, I do want to make the following statement: I am in no way hostage to anyone who would be an enemy of the Serb people. I myself are totally impartial, unbiased, and am governed by no one. You said earlier that the Tribunal is illegal. That is something that you have already said and you've put forward your arguments, that is your position. I must, however, tell you that we judges are fully independent and that we are in no way here to serve the interests of, as you put it, the United States or the European Union or anyone else. We rule on facts in the files and the issues at hand as impartially as possible. As you know, should a judge be biased or should you feel that a judge was biased you could object to said judge. I have also taken good note of what you said about Mr. Vucic, that he was acting on the basis of his political mandate, his political function, and that when he will assist you here in court he will only serve as your legal adviser. Mr. Seselj, yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Antonetti, not a single time did I raise any procedural objections to you personally as a judge. Ever since you started working on this case you have been working in a way which is proper to a maximum. However, your propriety in this case is not a sufficient reason for me to change my general attitude towards The Hague Tribunal. You know yourself that this Tribunal was not established in order to have justice carried out but in order to have peace in the Balkans, peace in the former Yugoslavia. That is what the founding papers of this Tribunal say. That is precisely the article of the Charter of the UN that was invoked. If I'm not mistaken, it's Article 7 of the Charter. I am not very good at numbers. So this Tribunal wants to establish peace. But not an impartial way, but a so-called pax Americana, that is to say a piece that suits America. Please do not try to convince me that this is an impartial Tribunal. If out of all the accused persons in this Tribunal, 75 per cent are Serbs, and 25 per cent are all the rest, Croats, Muslims, Albanians and Macedonians, then there is no argument for impartiality. Now, look at the judgements. The Serbs get life in prison, 40 years in prison, 30 years in prison. Croats get nine years perhaps or even less than that, Muslims two years, two and a half, five years, Albanians are set free, some Muslims are set free. As for the Serbs, the sentences are astronomical. There is no one who can persuade me otherwise. I know that a lot of crimes were committed on the Serb side but no one can convince me that Serbs committed more crimes than Croats, Muslims, Albanians or yet someone else. That is absolutely impossible. So, it is primarily Serbs who are being tried here. Serbs are the only one who are being punished Draconically, and now I'm supposed to stay that this Tribunal is objective? No. This Tribunal is not objective. It is not impartial. It is an anti-Serb court. As for everything that you have done in this case so far, Mr. Antonetti, I pay tribute to you. I don't know what your attitude will be in the future but so far your attitude has been honourable, principled, correct, and you have followed legal tenets 100 per cent. As far as I'm concerned, that is enough. I'm not asking for anything else. I am just asking for proper procedural rights to be exercised. I'm not interested in the judgement at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecution, I believe you wanted to address the Tribunal. Do you want to go back to public session or are you still okay with private session? I had after all mentioned Mr. Vucic's case in private session. What do you wish to do?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, briefly, we think that Mr. Vucic exploited his immunity as a member of parliament to engage in criminal activities that are inconsistent with his undertaking to the registrar, and we will be examining closely his undertakings and his behaviour and filing a complaint with the registrar to review the activities, to determine whether or not they are inconsistent with his undertaking. The other point I wanted to address was to request an opportunity to review Mr. Seselj's motion regarding remuneration of his associates. The Court had indicated that you would rule upon receiving his motion and we would like an opportunity to review it, to determine if there is an interest in the Prosecution to respond. I can imagine, perhaps, if the request is ultra vires the Statute it would be appropriate for the Prosecution to assist the Chambers in ruling on the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Fine. You know that the rules give you a fortnight to react. I would ask to you react as swiftly as possible. This is essential. And I will be waiting for your comments, although there is, in my view, no direct relationship but if you wish to reply to the motion, please do. I'm happy to have any comments on all these issues. Right. I suppose we should maybe switch back to a public session unless you have something else to say in private session, Mrs. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I agree that switching back to public session is correct and we'll review the motion immediately, and let you know if we're not going to file a response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Public session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Open session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something, Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, since we are in public session now, I would like to submit a request to lift confidentiality from the entire content of the private session that just ended because there were no conditions for having a private session. There is no jeopardy involved as far as documents and trials before this Tribunal are concerned, no other confidences are being infringed upon. What was discussed were things that are well known in the general public and since a certain procedure will be involved with regard to this matter only now, there is an enormous interest on the part of the public to know what happened during this private session and therefore, I ask to you lift confidentiality from that part of the session and to proclaim that part of the session public as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, does the person involved agree with you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you are referring to the person who was mentioned, that person certainly agrees with me. If you believe that he is the interested party. If I understood your words correctly. I can guarantee that he certainly agrees with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, on the issue of doing away with the private session, Ms. Dahl, any comments?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I have reservations of accepting that representation without the concerned party being heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, personally, I cannot really see any reason why we should remain in private session, but I would ask you to check with the interested party, whether this is indeed his position, and as soon as you have his agreement in writing, I will do away with the confidentiality of this part of our proceedings. So the issue will be settled but seeing we are talking about a private individual, and although I have no doubts that this private individual will agree with you, I think it is, however, sensible that this person should make their views known. So I would request that you should put the question to the said person and inform us. As soon as that is done we will publicise this part of our proceedings. Now, talking about something slightly different, the issue of witness protection, I recently gave a ruling on measures of protection to be taken by the registrar or the Prosecution when a name, when the name of someone, appears. Now, it may just happen that in the heat of discussions and debates, anyone may mention a name, including you, Mr. Seselj. The name might be that of a person that may be protected, that you wouldn't know, that I wouldn't know that the person was protected, and at the same time, the registrar, thanks to the e-court system, may notice that said person is under protection and therefore that should require redaction. It may happen that we may overlook such a fact in the course of our discussions and that a name may be mentioned. And sometimes the registrar or the Prosecution may not react immediately. It may also happen that the Court recorder may not spell the name right and that nobody really notices it in writing, that only people recognise it in hearing the name, but it might just happen that that person may be protected, may be under protection, and that we would not know it. So in that case, should that happen, the registrar and the Registry more generally should tell me, should inform me, whether there is a need for a redaction, even if the Prosecution hasn't noticed it. That's why I'm always very wary of giving names and I'm always referring to Mr. or Mrs., without giving the surname, and that in a way helps us avoid such problems. Which now brings me to something slightly different again, and that is Mr. Seselj's motion number 287, on Mr. Theunens's report, expert report. This is a fairly complicated issue, and I think it's time that we looked back at history to understand exactly what is happening. On the 28th of March 2006, the Prosecution filed a motion so that some parts of the Terrence reports would be made public 30 days before the beginning of the trial. Then, three witnesses would be called because they were mentioned in the report, witnesses 11, 26 and 31. And I shall only be referring to them by their numbers. On the 14th of September 2006, and in those days, Mr. Seselj, you had not attended the courtroom, and the stand-by counsel that had attended did not oppose the request. On the 2nd of November 2006, the Court ruled that the motion from -- filed by the Prosecution was null and void on the basis that as at the date of the ruling of the Chamber, the trial was meant to start within the next 30 days. Therefore, the accused should have, or so it seemed, had information and communication of the report in its entirety by then. On the 2nd of October, the accused received the ruling of the Court in B/C/S, but the report or the version of the report that was given to the accused was only a downsized version, whereas the Chamber had ruled that it should be the comprehensive version. And you received, sir, your version on the 17th of May, only a few days ago. It seems, when we look at this issue, that the Prosecution and yourself may not have fully understood that the ruling dated 2nd of October 2006 ordered for the full report to be handed over to counsel and not to the accused because in those days the accused was still only a member of the public. The complete report is in file number 22, and I'll come back to that later. So it does seem that we have something of a mess, that has to be sorted out, and I think we can settle that one with the assistance of Article 94 bis of the rules. Let me read out paragraphs (A) and (B) which in my view do settle the matter. It states, it reads, the report and all statements of any expert witness to be called by a party shall be disclosed within the time limit prescribed. "The full statement," it states, "shall be disclosed within the time-limit prescribed by the Trial Chamber or by the pre-trial Judge." So again it states, "the full statement", it's very clear. The accused must therefore receive the full statement and/or report, the full report in this instance. Paragraph (B) reads that "within 30 days of disclosure of the statement and/or report ... the opposing party" - in this case the accused - "shall file a notice indicating whether it accepts the expert witness statement and/or report; or it wishes to cross-examine the expert witness; and it challenges the qualification of the witness." There is, however, a qualification on this Article because we have here three protected witnesses whose identity should have been disclosed to the accused 30 days before trial started. As things stand today, the date for the opening of the trial has not been set and therefore we cannot understand when the 30-day deadline will start. Last time I had tentatively indicated that the trial may start in November, given the fact that the resources of the Tribunal would not make it possible to open a new trial over and beyond those currently running. Now, assuming the 1st of November may be the key date, the beginning of the trial, if you count backwards, 30 days before the 1st of November would be the 1st of October, and on that date, witnesses 11, 26 and 31 should be disclosed. Mr. Seselj, I believe, I expect, you have received the report because indeed report was in file 22, although you did not receive the entirety of file 22 but maybe some of your advisers or all of your advisers received the report, and from what I understand, part of the report has been redacted, although you were meant to get the entirety of the report. I will, therefore, soon rule on this issue, for indeed, I cannot see how you should give your -- make your position known on the basis of Rule 94 bis(B) if you have not received the full report. I'd like to ask you, Mr. Seselj, if you have looked into this issue, if you have a position and what you feel about it. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I got a redacted report -- version of the report, of the Prosecution expert witness, Theunens. Seven or eight pages were blackened, I think, I can't remember exactly now, and I handed this over to my legal advisers because they cannot receive any documents directly from the Registry or the Prosecution. I am the only person who can get documents and then, if necessary, I forward them to them. And on that basis, my legal advisers drafted this motion. So it doesn't have to do only with the redaction of the names of protected witnesses, specifically three names, up to 30 days before the trial begins. However, it is also the content that was redacted. The name could have been put under a code name, but they should have disclosed the content to me but they were not able of doing that. Of course, I'm going to state my views on the expert report in accordance with Rule 94 bis only when I receive it in its entirety. And what they sent to me, this redacted report, with seven or eight pages blackened, that doesn't mean a thing. It would have been better for them not to have sent it at all. You know, I don't even have the patience to read it if it's not there in it's comprehensive version, and I feel that they've blackened out the main points, and now I'm supposed to read what is irrelevant. Now, what is really building up the suspense on my part is what is it that is -- what is there that is blackened. So I cannot prepare my Defence properly. I think there has been great abuse in terms of granting protective measures for witnesses and for expert reports. Never has it happened that the Prosecution supported in detail its motion for protective measures. They use a single standard sentence and Trial Chambers routinely decide to grant these protective measures. Therefore, the situation is that there are almost more witnesses with protective measures than those testifying without protective measures. However, it is incredible that even as far as an expert report is concerned, which in essence should be a scholarly work, not testimony, not testimony by a fact witness, even within an expert report certain sections are declared confidential a month before trial. What can be so secret in an expert report? If it's a name, then the name could have been deleted and a code name could have been used. Nothing more than that. However, the Prosecution tendentiously deletes a significant part of the text, about 10 per cent of the text. I guess they are deleting the most important part of the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl, on the Theunens's report, Mr. Seselj has made his views known and he suggests that the best way to proceed would be to give him the full report and give -- either blacken or give a code name for the protected witnesses. There are all sorts of ways of proceeding. What is your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, we rely on our written submissions and I would note that the report itself is over 250 pages. The redactions are, de minimis, yet critical to the protection of the witnesses and I believe that Rule 94 bis has to be read in conjunction with the obligation of the Chambers to protect witnesses. We filed, at the same time as our response to Mr. Seselj's motion, a request for renewed reconsideration of the delayed disclosure request that had been declared moot because of the proximity of the trial date when the previous Trial Chamber ruled on the motion in the first instance. That motion is pending and we believe that the security concerns that justify the protective measures should apply in full force to Mr. Theunens' report. The purpose of providing the full report of experts is to allow the accused opportunity to make the decision whether he accepts or rejects the report or the qualifications of the expert. I think those decisions can be made fully informed by the large amount of information that has been disclosed to Mr. Seselj and that he will not be disadvantaged by removing the redactions shortly before trial as we had initially requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, now, dealing with expert witnesses and expert reports, maybe what I have learned firsthand might be of assistance to you, relating to the way the procedure in this Tribunal is. As you may know, these experts are not experts as we understand them in civil law cases. These experts are related to the parties. Prosecution has its own experts. Some of them are, indeed, remunerated by the Prosecutor's Office, and you too will be in a position to choose your experts should you wish to call experts, expert witnesses. These expert witnesses are appointed and chosen by the parties. The Bench does not play any role in this position. The only thing we do is to check when an expert report is being filed, whether the said expert witness is qualified and has the adequate expertise to write up this expert report. And that is why we always require a CV of the expert witness. The expert report is always made up of a number of things, first of all a document, in this case 250 pages long, with footnotes and therefore the expert report, as I said, has footnotes which sometime refer to the evidence list that you have under the 65 ter exhibits list. Now, as far as I know, the accused in the history of our Tribunal have always challenged the expert reports filed by Prosecution and none of them were accepted automatically. In a 65 bis -- in 94 bis(B), the accused may cross-examine the expert. What happens then? Well, the Prosecutor says that the witness is an expert, that they want to include the expert report and the preliminary statement in the case, and in that instance, the Prosecutor may then present a number of exhibits included in the report to the expert witness, so that they comment on it and the Prosecutor would say, "You have submitted this or that piece of evidence in page X, paragraph Y, do you confirm the statement? And do you really rely on this evidence to write up this or that paragraph?" And then the expert witnesses agree, and over and beyond the expert report, the declaration and the statement, the Prosecution will also want to refer formally to the exhibits included in the report. So this is what happens during the preliminary -- during the interrogation -- the examination by the Prosecutor. Then you cross-examine the expert. You will put questions to the expert, put forward your own documents and exhibits, to contradict what the expert witness and/or the Prosecution have said. That is what happens during the Prosecution's evidence review. Then, when the accused calls in his experts, the same happens. Your expert will put in -- put forward his report, the Prosecution will cross-examine your witness, and the Prosecutor therefore behaves as you had behaved when you were cross-examining the Prosecution's expert witness. This is what happens with expert witnesses when they come to testify on specific items related to the case in point. Now, as for the time that the cross-examination may last, or the main examination, Trial Chambers usually consider that there is no need for a first examination, but in Article 65 ter, there are provisions for a time or a period of time due for interrogation, examination. You, as the accused, have the same amount of time to cross-examine, five or six hours. In most instances, the expert witnesses will come for one or two days for the examination-in-chief, the cross-examination and the Prosecutor may then put more questions to the expert witness directly related to the questions raised during the cross-examination. So I think this in practical, slightly technical terms, is exactly the way these expert witnesses are heard by our Tribunal. Now, once the expert report has been acknowledged by the Trial Chamber in entirety or in part, as soon as it has been admitted, the Trial Chamber may, in the final judgement, refer back to the expert report. The Trial Chamber may or may not refer back to the expert report depending on how relevant the procedure is. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, there is a problem about this. This International Tribunal has taken over from the Anglo-Saxon legal system what -- precisely what is the most negative about it. According to our continental system it is the Court that appoints experts, thus experts are court-appointed experts. They produce expert reports in situations where either of the parties make a convincing request for expert reports to be made to begin with. Here, we have the Prosecutor producing expert witnesses. They are no experts. They are officials of the OTP. It's virtually the same thing as the OTP presenting themselves as experts in order to produce evidence that they could not possibly elicit from any other OTP witnesses. Precisely because they are unable to instruct their witnesses sufficiently well for them to represent their position in a convincing manner, they come up with these so-called experts who produce works of pseudo-scholarship to prove the positions of the OTP. Surely enough, I am going to be challenging all the OTP experts including Theunens but in order for me to formally state my position as to why I am challenging a certain witness, I must have the report in its entirety. I will be challenging the report, that much is certain, but my deadline will start running from the day I receive a report in its entirety. The number of Prosecution expert witnesses only speaks to one fact, how unable the OTP are to prove what they are out to prove. There were cases in other trials where an official of the OTP was called to give cumulative evidence of simply what witnesses on the ground have told him. This was used by the OTP in some cases before this Tribunal; I can't remember which exactly. And then the investigator would simply appear as a witness and say, "I was told this by that person or that by another person," without even specifying who or mentioning any names which is not serious in the least by way of an approach. However, it's up to the OTP to decide and we'll see how their witnesses, such witnesses, will fare in the courtroom and I can guarantee that they will not fare too well. I won't leave a single stone unturned once I start cross-examining them and I will shatter their so-called evidence. I myself will have at least as many experts as the OTP, and as usually, the OTP appoint one of their own officials as their expert, I will also be recruiting my experts from my own Defence team. If someone that I have in mind as an expert is now not a member of my Defence team, I will appoint them tomorrow. That's what I'll be doing first thing. And then I will task them with drawing up an expert report on a particular subject in order to parry this blow by the OTP as well, just in order to be able to show how grotesque the whole issue is becoming. However, let's go back to square one, what is really fundamental in this whole matter. There is absolutely no reason for the OTP to simply blacken so many pages of Theunens's report. If we have the names of three protected witnesses, take here for an example, they can be replaced bay code, a pseudonym, something that exists in the documents already. And then we can have the expert report addressing their alleged statements. What is the secret that is being concealed by the OTP that is buried within the body of the expert report itself? Is this some sort of a secret question? Is it just a hoax, possibly an illegal one, possibly something that runs counter to anything that that is here termed procedure. I can understand why they are trying to conceal the names of protected witnesses. I'm not challenging that. You've gone too far in that as well. However, you are now blackening out whole portions of expert reports under the pretext that you are protecting the names of certain witnesses. That is absolutely untenable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that you have -- the different parties have expressed their position vis-a-vis expert witnesses. Before we take a break I would like to mention an issue that we have already discussed and not yet settled. That is the issue of the 38 files. I think you -- all of you know what is in these binders, and it deals -- they deal with the lawyer that was appointed to assist Mr. Seselj. The lawyer handed over these 38 binders that all sorts of documents are included in them, some of them highly relevant to the accused and he should receive them. This is particularly the case about the documents that were handed over to this lawyer under Article 68 and 66 of the rules of our Tribunal. The lawyer that was appointed had been appointed in August of last year. Having then been appointed in August, a number of documents were handed over to him in August, September, October, November, December, until the Appeals Chamber admitted that Mr. Seselj was entitled to defend himself by himself. Now, of course, Mr. Seselj must have access to these documents that had been passed on to the lawyer, because they are highly relevant for him. I would therefore request that the Prosecution should write up a list of all these exhibits and documents that were handed over to the lawyer. I assume that the Prosecution has such a list. I've mentioned this before. We are talking about the documents handed over under Article 66, 68, and even the motions that the lawyer may have had copies of and that Mr. Seselj might not have. Once this list has been written up, it will be passed -- handed over to the registrar. The Registry will then look at these 38 binders and pull out from each of these binders the documents that are on the list, to hand them over to Mr. Seselj. Now, why should this be done by the Registry? Well, precisely because the Registry is unbiased, and neutral, vis-a-vis both parties. We cannot ask the Prosecution to do this, seeing as Prosecution may then be informed of a Defence strategy. In some of the binders, there are memos on points of law, for instance. So this would be giving Prosecution an illegitimate advantage. Mr. Seselj also told us that he did not want to look through all these binders. And therefore, only the Registry, because of its neutrality, can, on the basis of the list, hand over the documents to Mr. Seselj. These documents, under Article 66 and 68 are needed by Mr. Seselj to organise his defence, to prepare also the cross-examination of witnesses, and also to choose and appoint -- and call his own witnesses in due course. In -- it is therefore impossible for Mr. Seselj to be in the dark about these 38 binders, especially as the rules impose communication of documents. And therefore, the Prosecution must check and must know which documents were transferred and handed over to the lawyer as of August last year, and hand over this list to the registrar. Mr. Seselj, any comments on this issue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Judge, sir, I do have an objection as a matter of principle. I never recognised Hooper as my defence counsel. Anything that is in his possession cannot be used as a Defence document in my case and cannot be of interest to my Defence case. The registrar or the Registry cannot arbitrate in this and cannot be the one to judge what, if anything, of Hooper's legacy shall or shall not be forwarded to me. Maybe the documents disclosed by the OTP under Rule 66 and Rule 68 could be important documents, and those should be returned to the OTP. The documents produced by Hooper himself, while pretending that he was preparing my defence, might as well just be burned by the OTP. I'd rather end up in prison for 100 years than use anything that was done by Hooper as he was pretending to be defending me. I will certainly not be accepting any of that. As for what was disclosed by the OTP under Rule 66 and Rule 68, well, they must disclose the same thing to me. I can't have the registrar disclosing documents to me under Rule 66 and Rule 68. That is just not within their remit. This is something for the OTP to do and the OTP alone. The registrar cannot assume any of the capacities incumbent on the OTP, or any of their obligations. The registrar, acting under an official obligation, can destroy something, for example, that is found in Hooper's legacy, so to speak, and something that he believed to be strategically important for my defence, some notes that he made, some potential witness statements that he planned for my defence, or any observations made by any of his associates while preparing the defence. That would be totally pointless. I'm not opposing that. Maybe that too can be submitted to the OTP but it might be extremely unethical, even immoral. And that is why I think the registrar should just destroy that. However, whichever documents bear the OTP stamp, something that was originally submitted by the OTP, those might as well be returned to the OTP and then disclosed to me and then I will sign for those. However, there is another thing, the documents under Rule 66 and Rule 68 were disclosed to Hooper by the OTP on a regular basis in English. This is useless, as far as I'm concerned. Those must be in Serbian. So what's the registrar's job in this case? Should they check what has been translated and what hasn't? No. The OTP must serve all these documents on me in the Serbian language. Again, I'm pointing you to the document by the OTP, dated the 6th of November 2006. In item 10 alone, they say that 207.000 pages must be submitted to me in the Serbian language. They tried using the CD-ROM format and yet they failed. So now we need hard copies. 207.000. I'm deeply convinced that they haven't even embarked on putting all of this on paper and actually typing it up. When will they? I haven't a clue. I do know that the trial cannot begin without this, because all these are Rule 68 documents, potentially exculpatory documents which the OTP already have in their possession. And they must, as soon as they have those, disclose them to me. It is an obligation incumbent upon them. Otherwise you cannot have a fair trial. I have proved that you have in your possession 207.000 important documents, potentially exculpatory for my Defence. If you don't submit those to me, there is no fair trial. Don't think the trial can even begin until I have those. This is the most precious document for me. I want all 207.000 of them in my prison cell so I can go through them at my leisure, and judge which I can use and which I cannot. It is you who has established that these documents are potentially exculpatory, not me. This is something that you arrived at. Therefore, whatever you disclosed to Hooper was disclosed to no one at all, in purely practical terms. All the OTP documents go back to OTP. That is what I suggest we do. Whatever belongs to Hooper and was not disclosed by the OTP should just simply be burned which I think would be the most ethical course of action to take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj is raising an issue here which I had mentioned not last time but at a previous Status Conference. You are under the obligation to disclose to the accused, pursuant to Rule 66 and 68, those documents in a hard copy format, and translated in his own language. So you are under two obligations: A, hard copies documents and translated in his own language. I am just covering, because I had noticed this before and perhaps Mr. Seselj has made a mistake, the documents sent to Mr. Hooper, there would be 207.000 pages? If that is the case, if the 207.000 pages have been disclosed pursuant to Rule 66 and 68, these must be translated and provided in a hard copy, unless he has made a mistake. But this seems a huge amount of pages. Where do you stand in relation to this question, Ms. Dahl, because I remember mentioning this a while ago already?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: We agree with the Chambers that the privileged status of Mr. Hooper's documents should be safeguarded and it would be inappropriate to return material to the Office of the Prosecution and thus jeopardise any work product or defence strategy that might be contained in the material. We can produce the list of materials that was disclosed to Mr. Hooper during the point of time where he was representing the accused and we believe the registrar is competent and efficient to make the proper selections. We would indicate where we have already served on Mr. Seselj directly a duplicate set so that we are not asking the registrar to engage in needless work and we would also indicate where material in Mr. Hooper's possession was subject to protective measures or applications against disclosure to the accused. With regard to what falls within Rule 68, we are reviewing all of the prior disclosure in this case to make sure that we are in full compliance with the rules and orders of the Chamber, and as required, will make the necessary translations. It should be noted that Mr. Hooper was given material in its original form, if it was available, meaning the native language of the person who gave the statement. And we are endeavouring to make sure that Mr. Seselj has everything that he needs and is entitled to under the rules to prepare his defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl, Rule 66 states that the Prosecution is under the obligation to disclose to the accused in his own language all the documents that are going to be adduced or that are likely to be exculpatory material. The accused should have these in his own language and in a hard copy format. This is a legal obligation, and we cannot start the trial if the accused has not received these documents. That's a first point. Second, Rule 68 exculpatory material which should also be disclosed to the accused. When I listened to you, I think I understood that you disclosed to Mr. Seselj, you have already disclosed some documents to him, but the question I have runs as follows: From August onwards, which was the time when Mr. Hooper was designated, you need to ensure that all the documents you have sent to Mr. Hooper, all these documents, must be sent to Mr. Seselj, and this was in a CD-ROM format when they were sent to Mr. Hooper but these documents should be sent in hard copy and in B/C/S. This is where we stand. And it can't be otherwise. You gave an explanation, but I don't feel entirely satisfied with it. I want to make sure that the obligation you are under has been met, because if you have not met your obligation, you could be liable for Prosecution, and this is something you know full well. So I don't think we have to try to go into too much detail. I understand that you have a technical problem, if you have a great number of documents, and if you felt that the electronic format was a way of finding a solution here, no, this is not the case. As far as I'm concerned, Rule 68(A), Rule 68(i), clearly indicates that the documents must be disclosed in a hard copy format. The electronic format only pertains to a different category of documents, i.e. collection of documents and software packages, but anything relating to -- that were part of the indictment and were part of the investigation and which will be adduced at trial need to be handed over to the accused. Also, any documents mentioned in the expert reports. And this cannot be disclosed in an electronic format. Mr. Seselj has just told me that we are talking about 207.000 documents. I'm quite surprised. Are you quite sure? Are you sure the figure is right, 207.000 pages?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Judge. I am sure. I am sure because this is a Prosecution document. I don't know whether they are in a position to show it to you on the document. It was submitted to me on the 6th of November 2006. This is a survey of all disclosed or returned material, where it is established exactly what it was that I received because it was on paper and in the Serbian language, and what I refused because it was on CD and what was disclosed to Hooper and not to me. You can see all of that from this document. Now, only in one point, there are over 300.000 pages of documents here. Only in one paragraph, paragraph 10, four DVDs are referred to. According to Rule 68, 207.210 pages in the Serbian language. That is paragraph 10. If they were in a position to present this document to you on a monitor. This is a survey made by the OTP and they submitted this both to me and to the Trial Chamber. It was submitted to me on the 6th or rather the 8th of November, or the 6th of November, and the Trial Chamber received it in English probably a few days before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I've acknowledged what you have said and I shall look into the matter. For technical reasons, we need to have a 20-minute break now and we shall resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have resumed our hearing. Mr. Seselj, I must tell you that I was very puzzled by these 207.000 documents. Could you give me the document which you showed me in colour, to see what this document is? Usher, would you kindly go and fetch the document which Mr. Seselj had a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, sir, this document was disclosed by the OTP on the 6th of November 2006, pursuant to a ruling by the Trial Chamber. There is an overview of disclosed documents under Rule 66 and Rule 68. Let me draw your attention to paragraph 10 of the document. It's in Serbian. However, the OTP have the document in English because they certainly had it when they submitted it to the previous Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. In your own language I see that in paragraph 10, pursuant to Rule 68, 207.000 documents -- 207.210 documents. This is what I see here. This document is dated the 2nd of November 2006. Ms. Dahl, normally speaking, you should have this document in your own language, which does indicate that there are 207.000 documents. I give Mr. Seselj his document back and I would like to thank him for having enabled me to look at it. Ms. Dahl, what do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: May I ask for the document identification because the filing date indicated by Mr. Seselj is not assisting me in locating the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, does this document bear a Prosecution identification number?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On one piece of paper it says IT-03-67. I assume that that is my case number. However, there was an attached text of the OTP with this document but then I haven't got it here with me. But there must have been an English version too. And this was discussed at one of the Status Conferences in the month of November. Up here you have as the date the 2nd of November and that is probably the date of the document in English. However, underneath the text, it says the 6th of November 2006, which I assume means that the text was submitted to me in Serbian four days later. However, I can show this to the OTP if they wish and if it makes it easier for them to find it, if they wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Dahl can give you a copy. We can make a photocopy. And in that way you'll be able to find your way around it.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I can address the quantity of documents. I know that in the case initially, documents considered to fall within Rule 68 in the Milosevic case were tendered as disclosable given the theory of defence that was articulated by Mr. Seselj. Further to that, I don't have a particular response other than to affirm our position, which is that as the Trial Chamber's rulings now stand, electronic disclosure satisfies our disclosure obligations and on an ad hoc exceptional basis, we have been to facilitate Mr. Seselj's trial preparations and avoid the needless consumption of time discussing this objection, we have been giving him paper copies of material whenever possible, since my joining the case. If, upon review, there is the need to print out the material that fell within a different version of Rule 68 that was in play for the Milosevic case, and if the Chamber orders it, we will simply have those materials printed in paper but I want to make sure that the Chamber is aware of our position, that the facility to conduct electronic searches is a safeguard for fairness, and should not be dispensed with by this Chamber regardless of whether Mr. Seselj determines to use that facility or to disable himself and his ability to move quickly through documents to determine their relevance. My fear is that his objection is a strategic one and that upon delivery of 40 boxes of paper, he will then say he doesn't have time to read it all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Now, Rule 68, which is mentioned in the document, is -- includes two parts: "(i), the Prosecutor shall, as soon as practicable, disclose to the Defence any material which in the actual knowledge of the Prosecutor may suggest the innocence or mitigate the guilt of the accused or affect the credibility of the Prosecution evidence." That is little (i) and according to me, this should be disclosed to an accused who is representing himself. This should be disclosed in hard copy and in his own language. There is double small (ii): "Without prejudice to paragraph (i), the Prosecutor shall make available to the Defence, in electronic form, collections of relevant material held by the Prosecutor, together with appropriate computer software with which the defence can search such collections electronically." This relates to other relevant material, which is made available to the accused in an electronic format. According to your exchange of views, this would have to do with documents referred to in the Milosevic case, but in essence, in the Milosevic case, was there not material that could be considered exculpatory, that would suggest innocence or mitigate the guilt of the accused? I don't know. So it's for you to look into the matter and make sure you do it in a very accurate fashion because out of these 207.000 pages, I assume there must be all the records of the Milosevic case, all the transcripts. I don't know. But it's for you to look into it. I don't know personally. It is for me to check, to make sure that he has in his possession all the material likely to exculpate him, that may suggest innocence or may mitigate his guilt. You are under this obligation. It is for you to check out the document and see why it has been prepared in that way. We shall return to this issue but I think you have to focus on this particular question or pay attention to it. Mr. Seselj, I would now like to address another item which concerns you personally. I'm sorry, I hadn't seen you, Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I would just briefly like to refer to what the Prosecution attorney said in relation to the Milosevic case. Mr. Milosevic himself agreed to have documents disclosed to him in electronic form. That is what his legal advisers wanted. Soon afterwards, he realised that he had made a mistake but it could no longer be rectified. In his case, there were many complaints in terms of the delivery of documents. You can see that from the transcripts. Mr. Milosevic agreed that documents be given to him in English. He knew English much better than me but in my opinion, that was a mistake he made too. And then the OTP overdoes things. Since he himself agreed that documents be disclosed to him in electronic form, you were in a position to do that. I do not agree to that. I want everything to be on paper. So these are two very different cases. If we look at another case where an accused agreed to have documents disclosed to him in electronic form, cannot be a precedent for a case where the accused resolutely opposes that. Secondly, the very fact that you marked so many pages of these documents as potentially exculpatory material now makes it incumbent upon you to disclose on paper, in Serbian, all these documents. I'm not going to let you carry out a selection now and say, "Ah, we made a mistake. That's not exculpatory and we're going to -- do not interrupt me now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Dahl, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I would object. I would ask the accused to speak to the Court and not to the opposing party. I believe that is a breach of proper courtroom decorum and not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, on the merits of this, I think you're right, as far as form is concerned. I'd like you to address me and the Prosecutor would like the rules to be properly applied. So turn to me when you take the floor. But as far as the document is concerned, and that's what I'm interested in, thanks to Mr. Seselj, it's not the Prosecution that notified me of this. In the Milosevic case, the Prosecutor, pursuant to Rule 68, had disclosed to Mr. Milosevic in electronic format anything pursuant to Rule 68(i). Mr. Milosevic was conversant in English and the amicus curiae had accepted this system. This had not been a problem for Mr. Milosevic, but there is a problem -- this is a problem for Mr. Seselj because Mr. Seselj cannot accept this system. Something which had escaped me and where it is an issue is that in those documents which had been disclosed to Mr. Milosevic, there were exculpatory documents that could be of interest to Mr. Seselj, who is part of the joint criminal enterprise together with Mr. Milosevic. I think it is important to remember this. I have the indictment here in front of me, and in the indictment, in paragraph 8, all the members of the joint criminal enterprise are mentioned: Slobodan Milosevic, Veljko, Blagoje Adzic, Colonel Ratko Mladic, Jovica Stanisic, Franko Simatovic, Radovan Stojicic, Milan Martic, Goran Hadzic, Radovan Karadzic, Momcilo Krajisnik, Mrs. Biljana Plavsic, and the last one formerly Arkan, Zeljko Raznjatovic. So Mr. Milosevic was part of the joint criminal enterprise, as is Mr. Seselj, so the exculpatory material which you sent to Mr. Seselj may concern him also. He would therefore like to receive them in his own language. I hope these have been translated and he would like to receive them on paper. This is no mean issue. It is important you deal with it. We will certainly get back to this. It is incumbent on the Prosecution to look into this and deal with it and on the 4th of July, you must inform me of where you stand. I shall now move on to another topic. Yes, Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, if you look at the transcript of today's Status Conference as well, you can see that I invariably address you only. When I address you, it is the figurative way I speak and how I'm going to convey a particular message. For example, I can mention a witness and say, "You have to tell the truth and so on and so forth." So it's not that I was addressing the Prosecutor. I'm addressing you. And through you, as the Presiding Judge, I'm conveying a message to the Prosecution, and I am astonished by this absence of intelligence and inventiveness. How can one not understand that, invariably, I have been addressing you only and you can see that from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I acknowledge this because when you first intervened, you did say, "Your Honour" before making your submission, so Mr. Seselj was addressing me and was not addressing the Prosecutor. So let's set this aside for the moment because we have more important issues to address right now, namely the question of Rule 67, which is of great concern to you, Mr. Seselj. Lastly -- of late, I asked the Prosecution to draw up its list of witnesses and to update its pre-trial brief, but Rule 67 states as follows: "Within the time limit prescribed by the Trial Chamber or by the Pre-Trial Judge appointed pursuant to Rule 65 ter, the Defence" - i.e. you, in this instance - "shall notify the Prosecutor of its intent to offer the defence of alibi; in which case a notification shall specify the place or places at which the accused claims to have been present at the time of the alleged crime and the names of -- and addresses of witnesses and any other evidence upon which the accused intends to rely to establish the alibi." Thereafter, "Any special defence, including that of diminished or lack of mental responsibility; in which case a notification shall specify the names and addresses of witnesses and any other evidence upon which the accused intends to rely to establish the special defence." Therefore, Mr. Seselj, this procedure is made available to you. This contains two aspects: A, the defence of alibi; and B, any special defence. You may resort to this but you may also not resort to this rule. It is for you to decide. What is the defence of alibi? For instance, when an accused is told that he was present on the scene when in fact he was not there. In that case, the accused says, no, this is not right, I was not there, it wasn't me. So the defence of alibi deals with this kind of situation where somebody is alleged to have behaved a certain way or to be responsible for a particular fact when the person was not there. When you invoke this particular item, you need to specify the names and addresses of the witnesses in support of your defence. Then we also have a special defence which can bring together a number of things. I don't think this would apply to you, but if, for instance, we are dealing with mental responsibility, either the fact that the person is not able to understand things or that the accused has a mental disability. I don't think this applies to you. But this is something that an accused can also resort to. In that case, the accused can say that he was not able to understand what he was doing and therefore cannot have been responsible for those wrongdoings. Now, when this has been dealt with, paragraph (ii): "The Prosecutor shall notify the Defence of the names of the witnesses that the Prosecutor intends to call in rebuttal of any defence plea." In paragraph -- Rule 67 specifies that if you do not resort to this, you are still entitled to testify on your defence plea thereafter. Let me remind you that this rule does exist. If you would like to use it, it is for you to inform the Prosecution about it because the Trial Chamber has nothing to do with this system. It is for the Defence to inform the Prosecution.
